Even Einstein. He reshaped physics at 26, then spent decades resisting quantum mechanics — the framework his early work made possible. He didn't stop being brilliant. He stopped being disruptive. https://t.co/qRY3y4190F
Across 126 countries, younger workforces (China, India) produce more disruptive papers. Older ones (U.S., Japan) produce more recombinatorial work. https://t.co/efdjhxBvqi

Natural experiment: after mandatory retirement for U.S. tenured faculty ended in 1994, references in American papers aged significantly vs. a U.K. baseline (UK retained mandatory retirement until 2011). A well-meaning reform had a measurable scientific cost. https://t.co/xikR27FMbI

The pattern cascades socially. Papers reviewed by older referees gain older citations between preprint and publication. As fields age on average, even young scientists in those fields focus on older work. The churn of ideas slows for everyone. https://t.co/PlpaMwlcyd

Researchers also begin criticizing younger ideas right around tenurable age (~10 years from first publication). The shift from disruptor to gatekeeper is consistent across times and fields. https://t.co/riOVSnIt39

We trace this to the Nostalgia Effect: scientists cite older work as careers progress, ~1 month per career year. The paper that most anchors a researcher's career is typically published TWO YEARS before their own first publication. Imprinting that persists for decades. https://t.co/5sAGb9xv49

Capacity to discover new combinations among established ideas rises with experience as capacity to displace existing paradigms falls. Older scientists aren't less creative, but differently. Both enable progress. Only one clears space for new ideas. https://t.co/38czRsZuiY

The "does creativity decline with age?" debate has been muddled by a category error. There isn't one kind of creativity. There are two...and they move in opposite directions across a career. https://t.co/6Zt2YBug8j
